newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: SOCCER-UEFA AND CAF SET TO RATIFY CLOSER TIES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-UEFA AND CAF SET TO RATIFY CLOSER TIES.

text.p: UEFA and CAF, the bodies which control soccer in Europe and Africa, are expected to announce a series of wide-ranging proposals on Thursday aimed at strengthening links between the two continents.
The executive committees of both organisations met separately on Wednesday before their first joint meeting, scheduled for Thursday.

And while neither organisation issued any official statement, it appears Europe will provide Africa with money, technical assistance, coaching development and a number of other aids designed to help improve the game in Africa.
A source close to UEFA said: "The exact details need a little fine-tuning but in principle the two governing bodies will endeavour to co-operate far more closely than in the past.

"It is no secret that there have been times when Europe has acted against Africa's interests and the Africans have done the same to the Europeans. The time for that has past and we are now set on building bridges rather than creating more divisions between ourselves."
One of the proposals expected to be announced on Thursday is that some African federations will be sponsored by UEFA for either two or four years and aid will be provided for the recipient nation.

On the playing side, European trainers will help develop coaching in African countries, money will be provided to improve pitches there and international matches between African and European nations, a rarity at present, are expected to increase.

Wednesday's match between Europe and Africa was likely to be a one-off, or at best played every few seasons, but the new Under-17 tournament, which begins this week between four nations from Europe and four from Africa, will be held every two years.

While this week's initiatives in Lisbon are kicking off the European Union's Year Against Racism, they are also seen as a move by UEFA president Lennart Johansson to win African support for his bid to become the next president of world soccer's governing body FIFA when Brazilian Joao Havelange retires next year.

Johansson caused outcry last November when he admitted making a racist joke at the expense of Africans while at a meeting in South Africa and some observers feel that those remarks seriously harmed his chances.

But a high-ranking Confederation of African Football (CAF) official said on Wednesday he fully expected the African nations to support Johansson's bid rather than that of CAF president Issa Hayatou of Cameroon.
"The feeling among many people in our federation is that Johansson is the right choice but that no-one should stay in power for the length of term that Havelange has had," the official said.
Havelange, who is now 80, has been FIFA president since 1974.
In return for supporting Johansson, the Africans may stipulate that future presidents should be subject to a maximum term of office, giving an African the chance to head FIFA in six or 10 years time.
